nameStory: Johnson's Jumping Spider gets its name from the arachnologist who first described it scientifically. It's also called the red-backed jumping spider because of the striking red or orange patch that often decorates its abdomen, like a tiny superhero cape.
description: Johnson's Jumping Spider is one of the largest and most impressive jumping spiders you might encounter, though it's primarily a western species with very rare sightings in New England. These robust spiders are built like tiny athletes, with a compact, fuzzy body and proportionally large front eyes that give them an almost curious expression. They're active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs, and can leap several times their body length to catch insects or escape danger.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a row, with the middle pair noticeably larger and more prominent, giving an almost owl-like stare that seems to track your movement

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build with a fuzzy texture like velvet when viewed up close, distinctly chunkier than most other spiders

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Often displays a bright red or orange patch on the abdomen, though this can vary or be absent; body typically black or dark brown with iridescent green chelicerae (mouthparts)

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably large for a jumping spider, with females being particularly robust and substantial-feeling if handled

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops, often turning to face you directly rather than fleeing immediately like most spiders

habitat: In the rare instances where Johnson's Jumping Spider appears in New England, it's likely been transported from western regions and found in sunny, warm locations like south-facing walls, decks, or gardens. They prefer open areas with good sun exposure where they can hunt actively during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing and becoming active as temperatures warm, often seen sunning themselves on warm surfaces during mild days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be spotted hunting during daylight hours, especially in the warmest part of the day.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with mating behaviors and egg-laying occurring before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Generally inactive, overwintering in protected locations like under loose bark or in building crevices.

funFact: Johnson's Jumping Spider has color vision that's better than most mammals and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, allowing them to see patterns on flowers and other spiders that are completely invisible to human eyes.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the Bold Jumping Spider, but Johnson's tends to be larger and more robust, often with the distinctive red abdominal patch. Remember: if you're in New England and see a large jumping spider, it's almost certainly a Bold Jumping Spider unless you're looking at an unusually vibrant red-backed specimen.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this harmless jumping spider with the dangerous Australian redback spider (Latrodectus hasselti) - they're completely unrelated species that just happen to share some red coloring. Johnson's Jumping Spider is essentially harmless to humans and actually beneficial as a pest controller.
compareHints: Johnson's Jumping Spider is generally larger and more robust than the common Bold Jumping Spider found throughout New England. While Bold Jumping Spiders have white markings forming chevrons or spots, Johnson's is more likely to show that distinctive red or orange patch. The Regal Jumping Spider is similar in size but has different color patterns with more white and less red coloration.
